---
applyTo: "spec/**/*.rb"
---

# RSpec and FactoryBot

- Load every file in `spec/support` from `spec/rails_helper.rb` by uncommenting the generated line, e.g. `Rails.root.glob("spec/support/**/*.rb").sort_by(&:to_s).each { |f| require f }`.
- Put spec setup in `spec/support`, not in `spec/rails_helper.rb`, with one file for each gem or concern, named after it, each with its own `RSpec.configure` block, e.g. `config.include FactoryBot::Syntax::Methods` in `spec/support/factory_bot.rb`.
- Include `ActiveSupport::Testing::TimeHelpers` for every spec in `spec/support/time_helpers.rb`, e.g. `config.include ActiveSupport::Testing::TimeHelpers`.
- When a spec checks a time, or the code works one out, call `travel_to` on the example's first line, with a blank line after it, and match each time exactly with `eq`, e.g. `expect(post.reload.archived_at).to eq(Time.zone.now)`. Never match a time with `be_within` or `an_instance_of(ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone)`.
- Use `travel_to Time.zone.now` when the spec only needs the clock to stop. When the code depends on the date, pass a fixed time that tests it, e.g. `travel_to Time.zone.local(2026, 10, 31, 23, 59)` for code that works out the end of a month. Never pass `with_usec: true` to `travel_to`.
- Avoid passing a block to `travel_to`, e.g. `travel_to(time) do ... end`. Call it on its own line.
- Include `Capybara::RSpecMatchers` for request and feature specs in `spec/support/capybara.rb`, e.g. `config.include Capybara::RSpecMatchers, type: :request`, so request specs can check the response HTML with Capybara matchers, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_link("Hello World", href: post_path(post))`. When a gem's specs check HTML too, add its spec type to the same file, e.g. `config.include Capybara::RSpecMatchers, type: :component`.
- In request and feature specs, prefer a Capybara matcher for the element over `have_content` or `include`, e.g. `have_link`, `have_button`, `have_field`, `have_select`, or `have_css` with `text:`, e.g. `expect(page).to have_css("h1", text: "Hello World")` instead of `expect(page).to have_content("Hello World")` or `expect(response.body).to include("Hello World")`.
- When checking a select's options with `with_options:`, check one option on each line, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_select("Status", with_options: ["Draft"])` and `expect(response.body).to have_select("Status", with_options: ["Published"])`. Never list several options in one check, e.g. `with_options: ["Draft", "Published"]`.
- For a role or flag on the whole app, build the user with a factory trait, e.g. `let(:user) { create(:user, :<role>) }`. Give the user factory one trait for each, named after it and defined in rank order. Use a plain `create(:user)` for the User persona, who has no role.
- Do not add a user trait for a role on one record. Build a plain `create(:user)` and give it the role on the record, e.g. as the record's owner or through a membership. For a persona with more than one role, build the user with the trait for the whole-app role, then give it the role on the record.
- In request specs, write persona contexts only for actions where access depends on the user. For an action that does not check a user, e.g. an API with a shared token or a callback from another service, leave out persona contexts and write one `context` for each way the request can be authenticated, e.g. `context "with an access token"`, `context "with an invalid access token"` and `context "without an access token"`.
- In request specs, write one `context` for each persona whose role plays a part in the action, and for the User and the Guest, in rank order. Name each persona context after its role as `"as a <persona>"`, e.g. `context "as a user"`. Put the Guest last, as `context "when not signed in"`. Use `"as a"` only for persona contexts, e.g. `context "with a Turbo Stream"`, not `"as a Turbo Stream"`. For a role on the record under test, use "the", e.g. `"as the <record role>"`.
- In request specs, for a persona with more than one role, name each role, highest first, e.g. `"as a <role> as the <record role>"`.
- In request specs, when a context uses a record other than the one its persona implies, describe that record in a second argument to `context`, e.g. `context "as a <role>", "with a <record> created by another user"`. A persona with a role on a record implies the record it holds the role on.
- In request specs, set up each persona inside its context as a signed-in `user`. Define `user` and the records the persona needs in each context, never in the `describe` block above. Never define a `let` per persona, e.g. `let(:<role>)`.
- In request specs, the user may have a person's name, e.g. Jane Tester, but the context name must still give its role.
- In request specs, check the status of every response that is not a redirect with `have_http_status`, e.g. `expect(response).to have_http_status(:ok)`. Leave a blank line above and below that line.
- In request specs, check every redirect with `redirect_to`, e.g. `expect(response).to redirect_to(post_path(draft))`. On the next line, check the whole flash with a hash, e.g. `expect(flash.to_hash).to match("notice" => "Post was updated.")`. Never check a single flash key, e.g. `expect(flash[:notice]).to eq("Post was updated.")`.
- In request specs, make one request per example and check everything about it in that example, e.g. the change, the redirect and the flash after `post posts_path`. Never repeat the same request in several examples with one check each.
- In request specs, tag each action's `describe` block with `:aggregate_failures`, e.g. `describe "POST /posts", :aggregate_failures do`.
- In request specs, wrap a request that changes records in `expect { }.to change`, e.g. `expect { post posts_path, params: { post: { title: "Hello World" } } }.to change(Post, :count).by(1)` or `.to change { draft.reload.title }.to("New title")`. Use `not_to change` when the request must not change anything.
- In feature specs, use `RSpec.feature` named after the feature under test, e.g. `RSpec.feature "Post Publishing"`, and write each example as a `scenario`.
- In feature specs, start each scenario name with the persona carrying out the task, then what they want to achieve, e.g. `scenario "<Persona> publishes a post"`. Order scenarios by persona rank.
- In feature specs, write scenarios for what a persona can do. Do not write scenarios for actions a persona is not allowed to take. The only exceptions are a regression, e.g. a bug that let the persona do it before, or a critical action, e.g. a Guest must never see a draft.
- In feature specs, carry out several actions in one scenario, e.g. find a post, open it, publish it, then check it is listed. Do not write one scenario per request.
- In feature specs, put a `# GIVEN`, `# WHEN` or `# THEN` comment above each step: `GIVEN` for setup, `WHEN` for what the persona does, `THEN` for what they see. Write the comments in the first person, as the persona describing the situation and what they do, e.g. `# GIVEN I am signed in as a <Persona>`. Start a step with `# AND` when it follows a step of the same type, e.g. `# WHEN I open the post` then `# AND I publish it`. Leave a blank line before each comment, except the first in the scenario. A scenario may repeat `WHEN` and `THEN`. Keep the `GIVEN` steps together at the start, except a `GIVEN` that sets up a mocked response, which may go just before the step that needs it, e.g. `# GIVEN the newsletter service accepts the post` before `# WHEN I publish it`.
- In feature specs for an API, make requests through `client = ActionDispatch::Integration::Session.new(Rails.application)`, e.g. `client.post api_v1_posts_path` and `client.response`. Start each scenario name with the persona who owns the access token, or with the client when no user owns it, e.g. `scenario "API client writes a post"`.
- In feature specs for an API, authenticate the way the client does. When the API takes an access token, send it in the request headers, e.g. `headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer <token>" }`. Never call `sign_in`.
- In feature specs for an API, check the status and the shape of the body of every response, e.g. `expect(client.response).to have_http_status(:created)` and `expect(client.response.parsed_body).to match("id" => an_instance_of(Integer), "title" => "Hello World")`. Use composable matchers for values the spec cannot know in advance.
- In feature specs for an API, take the data for each request from the response before it, e.g. `client.get api_v1_post_path(client.response.parsed_body["id"])` after creating a post. Do not look records up in the database or reuse records built with a factory.
- When specs look for the same element on more than one page, write a custom matcher named after what it finds, e.g. `have_welcome_new_author_banner`.
- Always write a custom matcher when one spec checks that an element is there and another checks that it is not, and use the same matcher for both, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_publish_button_for_post(draft)` and `expect(response.body).not_to have_publish_button_for_post(published_post)`. Never check presence and absence with different matchers, e.g. `to have_button("Publish")` and `not_to have_css("form[action='...']")`.
- Give a generic matcher no arguments, e.g. `have_welcome_new_author_banner`. Give a matcher for one record the record as its argument and the suffix `_for_<resource>`, e.g. `have_publish_button_for_post(post)`.
- Define a custom matcher with `matcher`, so it works with both `to` and `not_to` with as little code as it needs, and check the element with a Capybara matcher in its `match` block, e.g. `match { |actual| expect(actual).to have_css("form[action='#{post_publication_path(post)}'] button", text: "Publish") }` in `have_publish_button_for_post`. When the matcher checks one thing, write only `match`, without `notify_expectation_failures`, because RSpec runs `match` for `not_to` too and the option would make it fail when the element is missing. Never write a separate matcher for the absence of an element, e.g. `have_no_welcome_new_author_banner`.
- When a matcher only narrows one Capybara matcher, e.g. adds a filter, write it as a method that returns that Capybara matcher and passes its arguments through, e.g. `def have_comment_select(locator = nil, **options) = have_select(locator, class: "comment_select", **options)`. Use `matcher` when it checks more than one thing or builds its own selector.
- Build a complex matcher from simpler ones, combined with `and`. Define each part as a private method inside the matcher, with a `have_` prefix and named after what the part is, e.g. `def have_welcome_heading = have_css("h2", text: "Welcome, new author")` and `def have_first_post_link = have_link("Write your first post", href: new_post_path)`, then `expect(actual).to have_welcome_heading.and have_first_post_link` in `match`. Never name a part after a Capybara matcher, e.g. `have_link` or `have_title`, because it would call itself. Only then add a `match_when_negated` block with one `expect(actual).not_to` for each part, e.g. `expect(actual).not_to have_welcome_heading` and `expect(actual).not_to have_first_post_link`, and pass `notify_expectation_failures: true` to both blocks.
- When only one spec file uses a matcher, define it with `matcher` at the bottom of that file, inside the top-level `describe` block, after the examples.
- When more than one spec file uses a matcher, move it to a module in `spec/support`, extended with `RSpec::Matchers::DSL` when it uses `matcher`, and included for every spec type that checks the element, e.g. `type: :request` and `type: :feature`. Keep all the includes for a module in one `RSpec.configure` block in the module's own file, and add a gem's spec type to that block when its specs need the module, e.g. `type: :component`.
- Keep the shared spec code for a resource, including its matchers, in one module named after the resource with a `SpecHelpers` suffix, e.g. `PostSpecHelpers` in `spec/support/post_spec_helpers.rb`. Never name it `PostHelpers` or `PostsHelper`. Name a module for generic matchers after what they cover, e.g. `OnboardingSpecHelpers` for `have_welcome_new_author_banner`.
- Give each helper that builds a simple view element a matcher named after the helper with a `have_` prefix, e.g. `have_unknown_value_tag` for `unknown_value_tag`. Put it in a module named after the helper module with a `SpecHelpers` suffix, e.g. `UnknownValuesSpecHelpers` in `spec/support/unknown_values_spec_helpers.rb` for `UnknownValuesHelper`, included for `type: :helper`, `type: :request` and `type: :feature`.
- Check a helper's output in its helper spec with its matcher, e.g. `expect(helper.unknown_value_tag).to have_unknown_value_tag`, and use the matcher in request and feature specs instead of checking the markup, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_unknown_value_tag`.
- Give specs in `spec/forms/` a `:form` type in `spec/support/forms.rb` with `config.define_derived_metadata(file_path: %r{/spec/forms/}) { |metadata| metadata[:type] ||= :form }`, and include setup for them with `type: :form`. Never tag each form spec by hand, and never include setup with `file_path:`. Do the same for any other spec folder rspec-rails doesn't know, e.g. `spec/components/` with `:component`.
- Build the records an example needs inside the example, and name the example after the path it takes, e.g. `post = instance_double(Post, published_at: nil)` in `it "returns the unknown value tag for a draft"`.
- Only write a `context` when several examples share setup that the other examples in the `describe` don't. Never write a `context` for one example, and never set up a default with `let` for a `context` to override.
- In request specs, the required contexts are the exception to these context rules: write each persona context, each authentication context, e.g. `context "without an access token"`, and `context "with a Turbo Stream"` even when it holds one example. Define the user and the records each persona needs in its own context.
- In unit specs, e.g. decorator and action specs, build a record with an `instance_double` that stubs only the values the code reads, e.g. `post = instance_double(Post, published_at: nil)`. Never use a plain `double`, e.g. `double("post")`.
- When an `instance_double` can't stand in for the record, e.g. the code passes it to a route helper or a form, build it with `build_stubbed`, e.g. `post = build_stubbed(:post, title: "Hello")`.
- Use `create` only when the code needs the record in the database, e.g. when it runs a query, or a request or feature spec loads the record by its ID.

- TODO: How to write factories, e.g. `create(:post)`.
- TODO: When to use traits.
